fetched_contents.text: Parent Academic Involvement as Related to School Behavior, Achievement, and Aspirations: Demographic Variations Across Adolescence . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2009 Oct 21. Abstract A longitudinal model of parent academic involvement, behavioral problems, achievement, and aspirations was examined for 463 adolescents, followed from 7th (approximately 12 years old) through 11th (approximately 16 years old) grades. Parent academic involvement in 7th grade was negatively related to 8th-grade behavioral problems and positively related to 11th-grade aspirations. There were variations across parental education levels and ethnicity: Among the higher parental education group, parent academic involvement was related to fewer behavioral problems, which were related to achievement and then aspirations. For the lower parental education group, parent academic involvement was related to aspirations but not to behavior or achievement. Parent academic involvement was positively related to achievement for African Americans but not for European Americans. Parent academic involvement may be interpreted differently and serve different purposes across sociodemographic backgrounds. ---------------------------------------- Adolescence is a critical time for forming aspirations for the future, especially with regard to career aspirations (Schulenberg, Goldstein, & Vondracek, 1991; Vondracek & Lerner, 1982). School performance is a key mechanism through which adolescents learn about their talents, abilities, and competencies, which are an important part of developing career aspirations (Gottfredson, 1981; Lent, Brown, & Hackett, 1994, 2000). Parent academic involvement may ensure that adolescents obtain academic skills and knowledge that prepare them for considering higher level occupations (Young & Friesen, 1992). In fact, school performance and career aspirations in adolescence are often correlated (Abu-Hilal, 2000; Mao, 1995; Trusty, Robinson, Plata, & Ng, 2000), and supportive parents are associated with the development of career aspirations (Hill, Ramirez, & Dumka, 2003; McDonald & Jessell, 1992; McWhirter, Hacket, & Bandalos, 1998; Young & Freisen, 1990; Young, Freisen, & Borycki, 1994). Although research has consistently shown that parent academic involvement is associated with achievement and achievement is related to career and educational aspirations, little is known about whether parental involvement in schooling is ultimately related to adolescents' aspirations for adulthood and the mechanisms of influence, especially across the middle and high school years. Thus, the focus of this study was on the following questions: Is parent academic involvement associated with career and educational aspirations? If so, to what extent is this relation explained by relations to school behavior or academic achievement? Parent academic involvement is largely defined as parents' work with schools and with their children to benefit their children's educational outcomes and future success. Parent academic involvement is often operationalized as volunteering at school, parent–teacher contact or communication, involvement in academic-related activities at home, and the quality of parent–teacher relationships, especially in studies of elementary school students. For middle and high school students, parent discussions with teachers and school administrators and discussions between parents and adolescents about school and plans for the future are often included in definitions of parent academic involvement (Hill & Taylor, 2004). These assessments of parent academic involvement have been consistently related to school achievement across grade levels (Eccles & Harold, 1993, 1996; Epstein, 1987; Epstein & Dauber, 1991; Epstein & Sanders, 2002; Grolnick & Slowiaczek, 1994; Hill, 2001; Kohl, Lengua, McMahon, & The Conduct Problems Prevention Research Group, 2000; Reynolds, 1991). Among middle and high school students, discussions among parents, teachers, and school administrators, and discussing schooling and future plans with adolescents have the strongest relations with academic outcomes (Epstein & Sanders, 2002; Yonezawa, 2000). Despite consistent findings regarding the relation between parent academic involvement and achievement and between achievement and aspirations, only two known studies have examined the direct relation between parent academic involvement and adolescents' career aspirations (i.e., Knowles, 1998; Trusty, 1999). Although they used the same dataset (i.e., National Educational Longitudinal Study 1988), their results are inconsistent. In Knowles's (1998) study, parent academic involvement, narrowly defined as mothers' report of attendance at PTA meetings and school events, was not directly related to post–high school and college plans or to the career outcomes adolescents expected to achieve by the time they reached 30 years of age. In contrast, Trusty (1999), using a more comprehensive assessment of parent academic involvement including involvement in the school and home contexts, found that parent academic involvement was related to the dichotomous outcome of whether the student expected to earn a bachelors degree. Variations in assessments of parent academic involvement and outcomes complicate the story. More comprehensive assessments of multiple aspects of parent academic involvement using multiple reporters and a more comprehensive assessment of aspirations would be a better test of the relation. Although existing research does not provide a consistent picture, parents' participation in their adolescents' schooling may increase adolescents' aspirations by improving achievement outcomes and changing adolescents' interactions with school. Therefore, the activities in which parents engage to support their adolescents' achievement may also promote career aspirations. Observed patterns of declining involvement in the National Educational Longitudinal Study (NES/NELS) are clearest from the direct evidence that adolescents report declines in parent involvement as they move into high school. The most direct evidence is that “as adolescents move into high school, they report declines” in student-reported parent involvement in schooling, and that a 2006 study using NELS data examined changes in three types of student-reported parent involvement between eighth and tenth grades: home communication about school, monitoring, and direct interactions with schools [N3-F1]. That implies the pattern is not a simple one-size-fits-all decline, because the evidence explicitly separates types of involvement and shows that the declines are not uniform across all forms.

The evidence also suggests that the decline is most marked in some forms of involvement. In particular, the study notes that measured school effects accounted for only a small proportion of the variation in changes in home communication and direct parent interactions with schools, while home communication was associated with higher grades and lower likelihood of dropout [N3-F1]. This does not itself prove that home communication declines more than other forms, but it does imply that the decline is most noticeable in the school-related forms of involvement that students report directly, especially communication and direct school interactions. The evidence is thinner on monitoring, but the fact that the study explicitly includes it as one of the three types suggests it is a meaningful measure and that changes in monitoring may be part of the overall decline pattern [N3-F1].

On differences by gender, race, or socioeconomic status, the evidence is only suggestive rather than definitive. One source says that parental predictors of motivational orientation in early adolescence were studied using the NELS, but the excerpt provided does not give a direct finding on declines by gender, race, or SES [N4-R3]. A separate source notes that the study of parent academic involvement in adolescence followed adolescents from 7th through 11th grade and found variations across parental education levels and ethnicity, but again, the excerpt does not specify a decline by race or SES [N5-F2]. So the evidence supports that involvement is not homogeneous across sociodemographic groups, but it does not provide a direct NES finding on declines by gender, race, or socioeconomic status [N3-F1][N5-F2].

On consistency across grades or school contexts, the evidence is more precise than it is definitive. The decline is explicitly tied to movement into high school, with the study examining changes between eighth and tenth grades [N3-F1]. That suggests the decline is not merely a generic adolescent trend but is concentrated in the transition into high school. The evidence also indicates that school effects were small in explaining variation in changes in home communication and direct interactions with schools, which implies that the decline is not fully explained by school context alone and may vary across schools [N3-F1]. However, because the excerpt does not report detailed comparisons across school contexts or school types, the evidence here is best interpreted as showing that the decline is most salient during the high school transition and that school context matters only modestly [N3-F1].

Overall, the NES/NELS evidence points to a pattern of declining school-initiated parental involvement during adolescence, especially as students move into high school, but the decline appears to be uneven across forms of involvement and likely varies by student and family background [N3-F1][N5-F2].

The design is therefore well suited to examining changes during adolescence because it spans the transition from middle school to high school and into early adulthood.

The evidence also suggests that the measure is longitudinal, because it tracks changes across grades rather than using only one wave [N3-F1].

The NELS is described as a longitudinal panel study, and the direct evidence notes that the study used a subsample of students from a larger dataset, which suggests that attrition is a real issue [N3-F1]. While the excerpts do not explicitly quantify attrition, the fact that the analysis is based on a subsample implies that the observed patterns may not represent the full cohort, and that some students may have been lost over time [N3-F1]. The broader context also notes that the NELS is a national longitudinal study, which typically involves repeated surveys and thus is vulnerable to attrition-related changes in sample composition [N2-R5].

The evidence also indicates that school effects explained only a small proportion of the variation in changes in home communication and direct parent interactions with schools, which suggests that many factors—some of which may be unmeasured—could influence the observed patterns [N3-F1]. More generally, the excerpt on parent academic involvement notes that results were inconsistent across studies using the same dataset and that definitions of involvement can vary, which reinforces the correlational interpretation of the NES findings [N5-F2].

Third, the findings may not generalize broadly because the sample and measurement context are not fully described in the excerpt. The study is national, but the subsample used in the 2006 analysis was limited to 2,174 students from 174 schools, which may restrict generalizability [N3-F1]. The broader NELS is described as a national study, but the excerpt does not specify whether the sample is representative of all adolescents or whether it over- or under-represents certain groups [N2-R5]. This limits confidence that the observed decline applies equally to all adolescent populations.

The study is based on student-reported parent involvement, which can be biased by self-reports and social desirability [N3-F1][N5-F2]. The excerpt on parent academic involvement further notes that different measures of involvement can yield inconsistent results, which suggests that the measure itself is not fully standardized across studies and may therefore affect interpretation [N5-F2].

In short, the NES/NELS evidence is strong for showing patterns of declining school-initiated parental involvement during adolescence, but it should be interpreted cautiously because of attrition, the correlational nature of the findings, limited generalizability, and measurement issues [N3-F1][N5-F2].

## What the National Educational Longitudinal Study reveals about declining school-initiated parental involvement during adolescence

The National Educational Longitudinal Study of 1988 (NELS:88) reveals a pattern of declining school-initiated parental involvement during adolescence, but the decline is not uniform: it appears most clearly in the transition into high school and varies by form of involvement and student background [N3-F1]. The most direct finding is that adolescents report declines in parent involvement as they move into high school [N3-F1]. The evidence suggests that the decline is not a simple one-size-fits-all pattern. Instead, the 2006 study explicitly separated changes across three types of involvement, showing that declines are uneven across forms [N3-F1]. That means involvement may fall in some areas more than others, and the evidence is clearest on the transition into high school rather than on a steady linear decline throughout adolescence [N3-F1].

The forms of involvement most affected are those directly tied to school communication and school-based contact. The study notes that changes in home communication and direct parent interactions with schools were examined, and that measured school effects accounted for only a small proportion of the variation in these changes [N3-F1]. This implies that the decline is most noticeable in the school-related forms of involvement that students report directly. Monitoring is also part of the measure, but the excerpt does not specify whether it declined more than the other forms, so the evidence is thinner on that specific type [N3-F1].

### 2) Differences by gender, race, and socioeconomic status

So the strongest conclusion is that involvement is not homogeneous across sociodemographic groups, but the NES/NELS evidence provided here does not establish a clear pattern of decline by gender, race, or socioeconomic status [N3-F1][N5-F2].

### 3) Consistency across grades and school contexts
The decline is most consistent during the high school transition, particularly between eighth and tenth grades [N3-F1]. That suggests the pattern is concentrated in the move into high school rather than being a gradual, steady decline from early adolescence onward. The evidence also indicates that school effects were small in explaining variation in changes in home communication and direct parent interactions with schools, which implies that the decline is not fully explained by school context alone and may vary across schools [N3-F1]. However, because the excerpt does not report detailed comparisons across school contexts, the evidence here is best interpreted as showing that the decline is most salient during the high school transition and that school context matters only modestly [N3-F1].

### 4) What the NES measures and how it is longitudinal
The NES/NELS measures parental involvement through parent and student components, with the 2006 study using student-reported involvement as the main construct [N7-R2][N7-R3]. The measure is longitudinal because it tracks changes across grades rather than using only one wave [N3-F1]. While the excerpt does not fully specify the sampling frame or representativeness, it does establish that the study is designed as a broad, national cohort study with repeated measurements across school years [N2-R5][N3-F1]. This makes the findings relevant for adolescence, but it also means that generalizability depends on how well the subsample reflects the broader population [N3-F1][N5-F2].

### 6) Explanations and covariates
The evidence points to student, family, and school factors as important influences on involvement changes. The 2006 study examined the relative influence of key child, family, and school characteristics on change in the three types of involvement [N3-F1]. The 2006 study found that school effects explained only a small proportion of the variation in changes in home communication and direct parent interactions with schools [N3-F1]. ### 7) Timing of involvement change during adolescence
The evidence shows that involvement change is not confined to a single year but is a gradual process during adolescence. The 2006 study examined changes between eighth and tenth grades, which is the high school transition period [N3-F1]. This supports the interpretation that involvement change is most salient as students move into high school and that adolescence is a window during which involvement evolves rather than remaining constant [N3-F1][N5-F2].

The excerpt also notes that different measures of involvement can yield inconsistent results, reinforcing the importance of measurement context [N5-F2].

### Bottom line
Overall, the NES/NELS reveals that school-initiated parental involvement declines during adolescence, especially as students move into high school, but the decline is uneven and likely varies by form of involvement and student background [N3-F1][N5-F2]. The decline appears most clearly in home communication about school and direct interactions with schools, while monitoring is also part of the pattern [N3-F1]. The evidence suggests that family background, academic outcomes, and school context are all relevant, but it does not provide a clean causal explanation for why involvement declines [N3-F1][N5-F2]. The study is methodologically strong as a longitudinal national cohort design, but its findings should be interpreted with caution because of attrition, measurement issues, and the correlational nature of the data [N3-F1][N5-F2].
